title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Sustainable AI** (Vol II). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

Power is an operational expense and a physical constraint on what can be built. A data center has a power budget determined by electrical infrastructure and cooling capacity; a training run that exceeds it cannot proceed at the intended scale regardless of its financial budget. Adding accelerators only helps if the site can supply their electricity and remove their heat. A design that runs efficiently on one machine can therefore become infeasible when replicated across a fleet.

nodes.label: Data Center Energy and Resource Consumpt

rows: **Power ceiling versus energy account**

A facility cannot draw more than its grid feed and cooling capacity at any instant, while run energy integrates average power over time, so a short run can be infeasible at modest energy and a long run feasible at large energy.
**Sustainability measurement contract**

An energy or carbon number supports a comparison only when it extends the reproducible measurement contract with five fields, the functional unit, system boundary, attribution rule, carbon signal, and time and location of operation.
**Operational carbon chain**
Operational CO2 = IT energy x PUE x grid carbon intensity, three terms acting at separate tiers, and PUE measures only non-IT overhead, so a coal-fed site can beat a hydro-fed one on PUE.
**Embodied carbon allocation**

Manufacturing emissions are fixed before first power-on and allocated to work by a declared rule, so their share of a job's footprint rises on clean grids and at low utilization and decides when replacing hardware pays.
**Dominant lifecycle carbon term**

Lifecycle CO2 is training plus inference plus embodied, where development multiplies training and inference recurs with query volume and idle capacity, so for widely served models inference is usually the dominant term and picks the lever.
**Carbon-aware placement and time-shifting**

Moving work to cleaner regions or hours changes the emissions factor, not the energy, so it must use a marginal signal from a forecast, meet deadline, data, capacity, and reliability constraints, and beat the cost of the move.
**Water accounting**

Evaporative heat rejection lowers facility energy at the price of water, so water is a separate, location-weighted account (WUE at the IT boundary, withdrawal vs consumption, direct vs indirect) traded against energy.
**Demand outruns efficiency**

Fleet energy is energy per job times number of jobs, and demand outruns efficiency twice, through scaling laws that price each loss reduction in multiplicative compute and through rebound, so efficiency targets need absolute budgets.
**Facility overhead boundary**

PUE is facility energy over IT energy, defined once at the facility boundary, so budgeting by accelerator TDP underestimates load and the boundary decides where each loss is counted: upstream transformer, UPS, and distribution losses raise PUE while supply and regulator losses stay in IT load.
**Energy crossover versus performance ridge**

Modeled energy crosses over from movement-dominated to arithmetic-dominated at an intensity set by energy per byte over energy per operation, a different point from the performance ridge, so batch-1 decode spends most of its energy moving bytes.
**Edge and federated energy accounting**

Local execution saves energy only when the radio, remote compute, and transfers it avoids exceed the device's added compute, idle power, and manufacturing, so edge and federated deployment move energy rather than remove it.
